The hard threshold at 0.5 is reasonable as a default—it's where the detector switches from thinking something is more likely real to more likely synthetic. For a detector with AUC=0.939, the calibration right at that boundary matters significantly, though this isn't necessarily problematic, just worth flagging. The ESS definition follows Kish's standard formula and correctly cites the PSIS work. For Proposition 1 on monotonicity, the claim is starting to come through but gets cut off. The proof handles edge cases where batches contain only real or only synthetic samples through the strictly increasing condition. The ESS monotonicity checks out—higher exponents sharpen the weight distribution. The dual constraints are properly formulated: a quality floor enforces α_eff(b) ≥ τ, a stability ceiling ensures ESS(b) ≥ n_min, and the optimal b* balances both requirements under the minimum intervention principle.

For conflict resolution, when the quality threshold b_τ falls below the stability threshold b_ESS, quality is binding and b* = b_τ. When b_τ exceeds b_ESS, stability takes precedence and b* = b_ESS instead. Now I'm checking the algorithm itself—it cleanly handles batches that already meet the quality threshold at b = 0, uses bisection to locate b_τ, verifies ESS feasibility at that point, and falls back to the ESS-binding solution if needed. Let me trace through the bisection logic more carefully to confirm it's finding the right boundary. \section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:experiments}

\paragraph{Training Data.}
We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo_2024_fineweb} as the real-data source.
To simulate web-scale synthetic contamination, we generate continuations with Qwen3-0.6B~\citep{yang_2025_qwen3}---the same architecture we pretrain from scratch---and inject them at ratio $\rho = 0.4$ via uniform random mixing.
This self-contamination design creates a challenging detection scenario where generator and trainee share the same distribution.

\paragraph{Detector.}
We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split, achieving AUC\,=\,0.939 with calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048 after temperature scaling ($T = 0.204$).
The resulting $q$-scores have mean 0.60, standard deviation 0.37, and median 0.71, with 46.3\% of samples in the uncertain range $[0.2, 0.8]$.
We use this lightweight detector rather than neural alternatives (e.g., ModernBERT at AUC\,${\geq}$\,0.98 in \citealt{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}) to test whether score \emph{calibration} matters more than raw discrimination for reweighting.

\paragraph{Training.}
We pretrain Qwen3-0.6B from random initialization for 6{,}103 steps (batch size 4, gradient accumulation 4, effective batch 16) with AdamW, cosine schedule (peak lr\,=\,$5{\times}10^{-5}$), max sequence length 2048, and bf16 precision.
All main comparisons use three random seeds (42, 123, 456).

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity (PPL) on a balanced real/synthetic test set via sliding-window evaluation (stride 1024, 4.08M tokens).
All evaluations are post-hoc with a unified pipeline; training involves no inline evaluation.

\paragraph{Methods.}
We compare five approaches:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Uniform}: $w_j = 1$ for all $j$ (no contamination handling).
  \item \textbf{Grid-$b$}: fixed $b \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0\}$, best selected post-hoc by held-out PPL.
        Represents validation-based selection~\citep{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}.
  \item \textbf{ESS-only}: $b^* = \max\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$, the maximum-intervention variant retaining only the stability constraint, ablating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
  \item \textbf{Golden Ratio}: $w = 1/\varphi \approx 0.618$ for synthetic ($q_j > 0.5$), $w = 1$ otherwise~\citep{he_2025_golden_ratio}.
        Requires known provenance labels (oracle).
  \item \textbf{Adaptive} (ours): per-batch $b^*$ from the dual-constraint formulation (\S\ref{sec:method}), with $\tau = 0.8$ and $n_{\min} = 2$ (half the micro-batch size).
\end{itemize}
